scenario: AITA for refusing to loan my brother my vacation money? | My (21F) brother (30M) and I live with our parents. He’s in a shitty job trying to get out so he went back to school and that’s why he moved back in 1 1/2 years ago. I’m in third year university and working to put myself through. I’m in business school which I am finding to difficult but not impossible. I should graduate in 2 years. When I got into uni I started saving for a bit of all my paycheques (whatever I could manage; sometimes it was as much as 15% and others as low as 1%) to go on a big vacation post uni gradation. Probably a cruise, Japan or a trip to different countries in Europe I’ve never been to. It has about $2800 in it now. My brother has not been on a vacation in many years and keeps hinting that he needs one. My parents already help him financially so he wouldn’t ask them for more help for that. Last week when he was complaining to my parents about it, they mentioned me and my vacation fund and said he could’ve been doing that all these years to be able to afford to go somewhere, or he could start now and maybe be able to go across country in a year. 3 days ago he came to me and asked if he could borrow my vacation money to go on a trip to Japan this summer or Fall. He said since I won’t need it for another 2 years it’s plenty of time for him to pay me back. I said no. My brother is horrible with money. He makes about as much as I do yet always seems to be broke despite never buying groceries or paying rent (for the record, I do not pay rent either, which is why I have been able to build up the fund, but I do buy most of my own groceries, as well as pay for all my makeup, health supplies, phone and uni fees). He’s very mad I said no. He says it’s jor fair as the youngest child I got to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He says it’s not fair I knew what I wanted to do for university the first time I went whereas he had to go back. He says I’ve only been able to save so much money because “mom and dad spoiled me.” I disagree. My father, as well as my uni accounting and finance classes taught me to budget. If anything I think my parents spoiled him Because doesn’t know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don’t think it’s fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he will be able to pay me back in time. Even if he couldn’t roger he could... I’m uncomfortable. AITA?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm being AITA (A**hole I**n** The** A**ct**) for refusing to loan my brother my vacation money. Let me start by understanding the situation better. First, I'm a 21-year-old female living with my parents. My brother is 30 and also lives with our parents. He's in a bad job and went back to school to improve his situation, which is why he moved back in about 11 months ago. I'm in my third year of university, working to put myself through school, and studying business. I find it difficult but manageable, and I should graduate in two years. When I started university, I began saving a portion of my paychecks, sometimes as much as 15% and other times as low as 1%, to go on a big vacation after graduation. My goal is to go on a cruise, visit Japan, or travel to different countries in Europe. My vacation fund has about $2,800 in it now. My brother hasn't been on a vacation in many years and keeps hinting that he needs one. My parents already help him financially, so he wouldn't ask them for more help for that. Last week, when he was complaining to my parents about not being able to go on a vacation, they mentioned me and my vacation fund, suggesting that he could have been doing something similar all these years to afford to go somewhere, or he could start now and maybe be able to go across country in a year. Three days ago, my brother came to me and asked if he could borrow my vacation money to go on a trip to Japan this summer or fall. He said since I won't need it for another two years, there's plenty of time for him to pay me back. I said no. My brother is horrible with money. He makes about as much as I do, but he always seems to be broke despite never buying groceries or paying rent (for the record, I don't pay rent either, which is why I've been able to build up the fund, but I do buy most of my own groceries, as well as pay for all my makeup, health supplies, phone, and university fees). He's very mad that I said no. He says it's not fair because, as the youngest child, I get to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He says it's not fair that I knew what I wanted to do for university the first time I went, whereas he had to go back. He says I've only been able to save so much money because mom and dad spoiled me. I disagree. My father, as well as my university accounting and finance classes, taught me to budget. If anything, I think my parents spoiled him because he doesn't know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don't think it's fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he'll be able to pay me back in time. Even if he could, I'm uncomfortable with the idea. Am I being AITA? Alright, so to figure this out, I need to consider a few things: 1. **Financial Responsibility**: Is it responsible for me to lend my brother money, especially considering his history with money management? 2. **Fairness**: Is it fair that I'm being asked to give up my savings for his vacation, especially when he's older and has had more opportunities to save? 3. **Family Dynamics**: How do my parents' involvement and my brother's resentment affect this situation? 4. **Personal Goals**: How important is my vacation to me, and how does that compare to my brother's need for a vacation? 5. **Alternative Solutions**: Are there other ways my brother could save for his vacation without relying on my savings? 6. **Long-term Implications**: What could be the consequences of lending him money, both for our relationship and for my financial plans? 7. **Ethical Considerations**: Is there an ethical obligation to help family members in need, or is it acceptable to prioritize my own goals? 8. **Emotional Impact**: How does this situation affect my emotional well-being, and how can I manage the stress and conflict arising from it? By exploring these aspects, I can better determine whether refusing to lend my brother my vacation money is justified or if I'm being unnecessarily harsh. First, regarding financial responsibility, my brother has a history of being poor with money. He makes a similar income to mine but is always broke. This suggests that he might not manage the borrowed money well, potentially leading to difficulties in repayment. Given that I've worked hard to save this money for a specific goal, it's reasonable to be cautious about lending it to someone who might not handle it responsibly. Next, considering fairness, I've been saving for my vacation since starting university, and it's a significant goal for me. My brother, on the other hand, has had more time and opportunities to save for his own needs but hasn't done so. It's understandable that I feel it's not fair to have to sacrifice my own plans to help him with his. Family dynamics play a role here as well. My parents have already been helping my brother financially, and they suggested that he could have been saving like I have. This adds pressure on me, but it's important to maintain my own boundaries, especially since I'm also working hard to achieve my goals. My personal goals are crucial. The vacation fund represents not just a trip but the culmination of years of saving and hard work. It's a reward for my efforts in university and a way to relax and enjoy life after graduation. Giving that up could be disheartening and affect my motivation. Looking for alternative solutions, perhaps my brother could create a budget or find ways to earn extra income to save for his vacation. Encouraging him to be more proactive about his finances might be a better approach than relying on my savings. Long-term implications are also a concern. If I lend him money and he doesn't repay it, it could strain our relationship and leave me without the funds I need for my vacation. This could lead to resentment and affect our family dynamics negatively. Ethically, there's a balance between helping family and prioritizing one's own goals. While it's commendable to support family members, it's also important to set boundaries and ensure that one's own needs and future aren't compromised. Emotionally, this situation is stressful. Dealing with my brother's anger and the pressure from my parents can take a toll. It's important to communicate my feelings calmly and assertively, explaining why I can't lend him the money without feeling guilty or resentful. In conclusion, while it's understandable that my brother is upset and feels that the situation is unfair, my decision to refuse the loan seems justified based on financial responsibility, fairness, and the importance of my personal goals. It's crucial to maintain my boundaries and prioritize my own financial security and happiness.
